what_it_does: CXL (Compute Express Link) is a new high-speed electrical interface that lets a computer connect extra memory chips — essentially plugging additional RAM onto the motherboard via a fast cable rather than soldering it directly to the memory controller. This extra memory is slower to access (2-3 times higher latency) than the main RAM, so the operating system needs to track which data is 'hot' (accessed frequently) and move it to the faster memory tier, while less-used data stays in the slower CXL-attached memory. Existing approaches track accesses using counters inside the CPU, but these counters confuse 'warm' data (moderately used) with 'hot' data (very frequently used), leading to bad migration decisions. M5 puts the tracking hardware inside the CXL controller itself, which sees every single access to the slower memory as data flows across the CXL link, giving a much more precise and complete picture. It also tracks access patterns at a finer grain — down to 64-byte chunks rather than full 4KB pages — so it can promote just the heavily-used portions of a page without migrating the whole thing.
